title: How Comas Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how comas work. They open with the story of Patricia White Bull, who woke after sixteen years in a coma, and Sunny von Bulow, who remained in a coma for decades. They cover the etymology of "coma," the three main brain parts (cerebrum, cerebellum, brain stem), and related altered states: vegetative state, stupor, and locked-in syndrome. They discuss causes such as brain injury, diabetes, meningitis, and drug overdose, and how doctors assess coma with the Glasgow Coma Scale and Rancho Los Amigos scale. They also cover diagnostic imaging (EEG, MRI, fMRI, CT), long-term care such as tracheotomy and physical therapy, and Adrian Owen's 2006 fMRI study on consciousness in comatose and vegetative patients. The episode ends with listener mail: corrections about dragon skin armor and EEG versus MRI for epilepsy diagnosis.

segments.title: Opening sponsor reads and banter
segments.summary: Sponsor reads for the Camry and GoDaddy, followed by hosts' banter about their bad day and a diet cherry Coke mix-up.

segments.title: Patricia White Bull and Sunny von Bulow
segments.summary: Hosts recount Patricia White Bull's sixteen-year coma after a C-section complication and her sudden waking, and compare her case with Sunny von Bulow, who remained in a coma for decades.

segments.title: Coma etymology and the brain
segments.summary: Chuck explains that 'coma' comes from a Greek word meaning sleep, which is misleading because comatose patients do not wake. The hosts outline the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brain stem and how they communicate.

segments.title: Vegetative state, stupor, and locked-in syndrome
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish coma from the vegetative state, which has sleep-wake cycles and brainstem-driven eye movements. They mention stupor and describe locked-in syndrome, using Jean-Dominique Bauby's book as an example.

segments.title: Causes of coma and diagnosis
segments.summary: Causes discussed include severe head trauma, diabetes, meningitis, and drug overdose. Doctors check alertness with the Glasgow Coma Scale and Rancho Los Amigos scale, scoring from three to fifteen, and use EEG, MRI, fMRI, and CT scans.

segments.title: Long-term care and Owen's consciousness study
segments.summary: Long-term care includes feeding tubes, tracheotomy, and physical therapy. The hosts discuss Adrian Owen's 2006 fMRI study at Cambridge University, which found similar brain activity in a healthy person and a vegetative patient, and the link between early GCS scores and prognosis.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Corrections include dragon skin armor, which was missed in the body armor episode, and a correction that EEG rather than MRI is used to diagnose epilepsy. The hosts close with a website plug and sponsor read.
